title: Review: Circulatory systems and blood vessels; Gas exchange surfaces and SA:V in organisms; Water
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM01a#t4 term and clue written for the game; BM01a#t1 term and clue written for the game; EX01b#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM01a#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM01a#N.5b, EX01a#N.7a, EX01b#N.5, EX05#N.8, BM01a#N.9b, EX01b#N.11, EX05#N.18, BM01a#N.4a, EX01b#N.3, EX05#N.11, BM01a#N.10. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Hydrophobic
items.clue: Describes non-polar molecules such as oils, which water molecules exclude

items.label: Dipole
items.clue: A molecule with one partly negative end and one partly positive end, as in bent H₂O

items.label: Fick's law
items.clue: Diffusion rate is proportional to area × difference in concentration, divided by thickness

items.label: Hydrogen bond
items.clue: Weak attraction between the δ+ atom of one water molecule and the oxygen of another molecule

questions.stem: The model shows three water molecules. The symbols δ+ and δ− show partial charges. Which statement correctly describes the interaction labelled 2 in the model?

options.text: An attraction between the partially positive H of one molecule and the partially negative O of another
A covalent bond in which the H atom of one molecule shares a pair of electrons with the O atom of another
An ionic bond between an H⁺ ion in one molecule and an O²⁻ ion in a second, neighbouring molecule
A strong bond, stronger than line 1, that holds the two water molecules in a fixed position

questions.stem: Why does gas exchange become a greater challenge as organisms increase in size?

options.text: The surface area-to-volume ratio increases, so far more gas has to cross each unit of the exchange surface.
The surface area-to-volume ratio decreases, and the distance from the centre of the organism to its exterior increases.
Only animals with lungs or gills exchange gases, so the challenge arises once an organism is big enough to have them.
A large organism uses more oxygen in total; the distance gases must diffuse to reach its cells makes no difference.

questions.explanation: Proportionally less surface supplies each unit of volume, and inner cells are too far away for diffusion alone. Both make specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems necessary.

questions.stem: Suppose that blood flow through the gill capillaries of an anaesthetised fish is stopped while water continues to flow over the gills, and that oxygen uptake across the gills falls almost to zero within a minute. Which explanation is best supported?

options.text: With no blood flow, oxygen built up in the stationary blood until its concentration matched the water's, so the gradient was lost.
Stopping blood flow cannot affect the gradient across the gill; the water flowing over the gills must have run out of oxygen.
Blood held still in the capillaries should load more fully, so the fall must have been caused by damage to the gill surface.
Oxygen enters with water absorbed into the blood, and once the blood stopped moving no more water could be taken up.

questions.stem: What is the role of the elastic tissue in the wall of an artery?

options.text: It contracts in waves behind the blood to push it along the artery towards the tissues.
It makes the wall stiff and rigid so that the high pressure cannot burst the artery.
It stretches during systole and recoils during diastole, maintaining pressure.
It forms flaps that actively open and shut to push blood forwards along the artery.

questions.explanation: Stretching during ventricular contraction stores energy; recoil returns it while the ventricle relaxes, keeping blood moving and pressure high between beats.

questions.stem: Glucose is carried dissolved in blood plasma and in phloem sap, and it is broken down by enzymes in the aqueous cytoplasm. Which property of glucose makes this possible?

options.text: It separates into positive and negative ions in water.
It is a small molecule, and small molecules dissolve readily.
Its many hydroxyl (–OH) groups form hydrogen bonds with water.
Water breaks its covalent bonds, splitting it into soluble fragments.

questions.explanation: The polar –OH groups of glucose hydrogen-bond with water, so glucose is hydrophilic and dissolves. It can then be transported in plasma and phloem sap and acted on by enzymes in solution.

questions.stem: Lungless salamanders have no lungs and, as adults, no gills. They exchange gases across their skin and the lining of the mouth. Which set of features would best suit this way of life?

options.text: Dry, thick skin, so that gases cross it as gases without having to dissolve first.
Thin, moist skin over a dense capillary network, with blood flowing through it continuously.
A large, bulky body, so that the total area of skin available for gas exchange is as large as possible.
Slow blood flow through the skin, so that each red blood cell has time to fill with oxygen.

questions.stem: With age, the walls of large arteries lose elastic tissue and become stiffer. Blood pressure in an arm artery is measured at its highest (as the ventricle contracts) and its lowest (between beats). What change in these readings is expected?

options.text: The readings become steadier, because a stiff wall resists the surges better than a stretchy one.
The highest reading rises and the lowest falls: the swing in pressure gets bigger.
The lowest reading falls to zero, because nothing keeps blood under pressure between beats.
No change, because the muscle in the artery wall contracts with each beat to keep the pressure steady.

questions.stem: Why is each covalent bond between oxygen and hydrogen in a water molecule polar?

options.text: The shared electrons are drawn more strongly towards the oxygen atom.
Each hydrogen atom gives up its electron completely to the oxygen atom.
It is a hydrogen bond, and hydrogen bonds are polar by their nature.
Oxygen and hydrogen atoms behave as opposite magnetic poles.

questions.explanation: Oxygen attracts the shared electron pair more strongly than hydrogen does, so the electrons are shared unequally: oxygen becomes δ− and each hydrogen δ+.

questions.stem: A model exchange surface is changed. Its surface area is doubled and its thickness is tripled. The difference in concentration does not change. By what factor does the rate of diffusion change?
questions.explanation: Rate ∝ area ÷ thickness here, so the factor is 2 ÷ 3 = 0.67. The extra thickness outweighs the extra area.

questions.stem: A muscle receives blood through a network of thousands of capillaries rather than through a single vessel of the same total volume. What is the advantage of this arrangement for exchange?

options.text: A single wide vessel would have more wall area than thousands of narrow ones, so exchange inside it would be faster.
The narrow capillaries force the blood through faster, so more oxygen is delivered to the muscle each second.
Each capillary has fenestrations, which are needed so that cells can pass out of the blood into the muscle.
The total surface area of the many narrow, branching vessels is far larger, and all the blood is close to a wall.

questions.stem: In blood plasma, glucose travels freely dissolved. Cholesterol does not: it travels inside lipoprotein particles whose outer surface carries polar and charged groups. Why does cholesterol need this carrier?

options.text: Cholesterol molecules are too large to fit between water molecules and dissolve.
Water molecules push cholesterol away with a repulsive force between them.
Cholesterol is largely non-polar, so it forms few attractions with water.
Glucose splits into ions in water, but cholesterol stays as whole molecules.

questions.explanation: With almost no δ+ or δ− regions, cholesterol cannot hydrogen-bond with water; it is hydrophobic. The carrier's polar, charged surface is attracted to water and carries the cholesterol through the plasma.
